\section[initium, initiī]{initium, initiī — a beginning}

\label{lesson:LA-C296-initium}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Latin for early, then the Latin for a little while ago.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: initium, initiī}
\textbf{initium, initiī} — \textquotedblleft{}a beginning\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Initium fābulae laetum erat, fīnis trīstis.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{The beginning of the story was happy, the end sad.}
\end{quote}

Neuter, 2nd declension. \emph{Initiō}: at the start. English \emph{initial}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{initium} is built on \emph{ineō}, \textquotedblleft{}to go in, to begin\textquotedblright{}, from \emph{in} and \emph{eō}, \textquotedblleft{}to go\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB): the going-in. English \emph{initial} and \emph{initiate} come from it.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{initium, initiī}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{initium, initiī}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{initium, initiī}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Latin for early, then the Latin for a little while ago, then say \emph{initium, initiī} again
\end{itemize}

\section[prīncipium, prīncipiī]{prīncipium, prīncipiī — a start, an origin}

\label{lesson:LA-C296-principium}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Latin for a little while ago, then the Latin for a beginning.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: prīncipium, prīncipiī}
\textbf{prīncipium, prīncipiī} — \textquotedblleft{}a start, an origin\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Ā prīncipiō rem tōtam nārrāvit.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{He told the whole affair from the start.}
\end{quote}

Neuter, 2nd declension. \emph{Ā prīncipiō}: from the start. English \emph{principle}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{prīncipium} is built on \emph{prīnceps}, \textquotedblleft{}first, the one who takes first place\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB): what comes first. English \emph{principle} comes from it through French.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\section[exitus, exitūs]{exitus, exitūs — a way out; an outcome, an end}

\label{lesson:LA-C296-exitus}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Latin for a beginning, then the Latin for a start.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: exitus, exitūs}
\textbf{exitus, exitūs} — \textquotedblleft{}a way out; an outcome, an end\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Nēmō exitum reī prōvidēre poterat.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{Nobody could foresee the outcome of the affair.}
\end{quote}

Masculine, 4th declension, from \emph{exeō}, 'to go out'. English \emph{exit}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{exitus} is built on \emph{exeō}, \textquotedblleft{}to go out\textquotedblright{}, from \emph{ex} and \emph{eō}, \textquotedblleft{}to go\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB): a going out, and so the way a thing comes out. English \emph{exit} is from the same verb.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\section[intervallum, intervallī]{intervallum, intervallī — a gap, an interval}

\label{lesson:LA-C296-intervallum}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Latin for a start, then the Latin for a way out.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: intervallum, intervallī}
\textbf{intervallum, intervallī} — \textquotedblleft{}a gap, an interval\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Post breve intervallum nūntius alter vēnit.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{After a short interval a second messenger came.}
\end{quote}

Neuter. First the space between two stakes of a rampart, then any gap in space or time.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{intervallum} joins \emph{inter}, \textquotedblleft{}between\textquotedblright{}, and \emph{vallum}, \textquotedblleft{}rampart, palisade\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB): the space between the stakes. English \emph{interval} comes from it through French.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}

\section[mōmentum, mōmentī]{mōmentum, mōmentī — a moment; weight, importance}

\label{lesson:LA-C296-momentum}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Latin for a way out, then the Latin for a gap.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: mōmentum, mōmentī}
\textbf{mōmentum, mōmentī} — \textquotedblleft{}a moment; weight, importance\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Mōmentō temporis omnia mūtāta sunt.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{In a moment of time everything was changed.}
\end{quote}

Neuter. A slight movement that tips the scales, then an instant, and also 'weight, importance'. English \emph{moment}, \emph{momentum}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{mōmentum} is built on \emph{moveō}, \textquotedblleft{}to move\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB): a movement, the tilt of a balance, and so an instant. English \emph{moment} and \emph{momentum} come from it.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}
